purpose: Sirolimus is most commonly used to prevent your body from rejecting a transplanted kidney. It is also used to treat a rare lung disease called lymphangioleiomyomatosis (LAM). Your doctor may sometimes prescribe it for other conditions as well.
how_it_works: Your immune system normally attacks things it does not recognize, which can include a transplanted organ. Sirolimus works by calming down your immune system so it does not attack the new organ. It does this by blocking a specific protein in your body called mTOR, which helps control how immune cells grow and multiply.
common_side_effects: Some common side effects include mouth sores, acne, upset stomach, diarrhea, headache, joint pain, and swelling in your legs or feet. You may also notice that cuts or wounds heal more slowly than usual. Your cholesterol and blood sugar levels may go up, so your doctor will monitor these regularly.
warnings: Because this medicine lowers your immune system, you are more likely to get infections, including serious ones. Avoid contact with sick people and wash your hands often. It can also increase your risk of certain cancers, especially skin cancer, so use sunscreen and cover up in the sun. Do not take sirolimus with grapefruit juice, as it can raise the drug level in your blood to unsafe levels. Tell your doctor right away if you develop fever, trouble breathing, or any signs of infection.
typical_dosing: The dose is different for each person and depends on your weight, the condition being treated, and your blood levels of the medication. Your doctor will do regular blood tests to make sure you have the right amount of the drug in your body. It is usually taken by mouth once a day, at the same time each day, with or without food — but always the same way each time.
